Title: La nueva estrategia de la UE para reforzar su defensa económica

Summary: 
The European Commission unveiled a new economic security strategy on December 3, 2025, aimed at anticipating global trade risks and strengthening the EU’s market resilience amid rising geopolitical tensions, particularly with China. The strategy emphasizes proactive risk assessment and enhanced defenses against external threats, especially from third countries. It responds to recent incidents, including China’s pressure to restrict rare earth exports and its blockade of automotive chips destined for the Dutch company Nexperia, a critical node in the EU’s supply chain. Maros Sefcovic, EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, stated, 'Europe remains a champion of open trade and global investment, but openness without security becomes vulnerability.' The strategy focuses on reducing critical dependencies in essential raw materials, technological components, and semiconductors—areas increasingly used by China as geopolitical leverage. The EU will integrate security considerations into trade defense investigations and strengthen existing tools such as foreign investment screening, subsidy reviews, and anti-coercion mechanisms introduced in 2023. Measures include combating predatory practices and industrial espionage, with enhanced scrutiny of strategic physical and digital infrastructure. Sefcovic emphasized the need for improved economic intelligence sharing across EU member states and industry to ensure synchronized action. While the strategy outlines priorities for quantum technology and critical services—such as favoring European or allied financing and limiting reliance on high-risk quantum or cloud providers—it does not yet include concrete proposals for funding gaps in emerging sectors. A senior official warned that strategic technologies are leaving European ownership 'not for good reasons.' In markets dominated by China, such as electric vehicle batteries, the EU seeks greater technology exchange and private-sector involvement, as 'that is where real risk is generated.' The EU already has emergency legislation from the pandemic and the Russia-Ukraine war to maintain essential goods, services, and personnel flows. A new advisory group with industry representatives will be established to strengthen this framework. The Commission also aims to build partnerships with countries facing similar threats, including Japan and EU candidate nations, as part of a broader effort to counter China’s growing influence in a fragmented global trading landscape.

Title: EU Greenlights Mandatory FDI Screening Overhaul

Summary: 
The European Union has reached a provisional agreement to overhaul its foreign direct investment (FDI) screening framework, requiring all member states to maintain mandatory screening regimes with a common minimum scope covering sensitive sectors such as defence, dual-use items, 'hyper-critical' technologies (including AI, quantum, and semiconductors), critical raw materials, energy, transport, digital infrastructure, electoral systems, and certain financial market entities. The reform enhances cooperation between national authorities and the European Commission, introduces procedural harmonization—including standardized review deadlines—and enables digital tools such as a potential single electronic filing portal and an EU-level database of past screening outcomes. Decision-making remains with individual member states, and the Commission does not gain veto power. The new rules will apply 18 months after entry into force, allowing time for national alignment. The framework expands cooperation to include intra-EU acquisitions by non-EU-controlled subsidiaries and strengthens transparency by requiring member states to justify decisions, especially when disagreeing with EC opinions. Despite improvements in predictability and coordination, national differences will persist, and key uncertainties remain, including the treatment of greenfield investments, retroactive reviews, and stock exchange transactions. The changes are part of a broader EU Economic Security Strategy, which emphasizes risk assessments around critical technologies, data access, and strategic inputs, with further measures expected on export controls, foreign subsidies, and outbound investment restrictions. Investors are advised to conduct early risk assessments and develop multijurisdictional filing strategies.

The framework expands cooperation to include intra-EU acquisitions by non-EU-controlled subsidiaries and strengthens transparency by requiring member states to justify decisions, especially when disagreeing with EC opinions. Despite improvements in predictability and coordination, national differences will persist, and key uncertainties remain, including the treatment of greenfield investments, retroactive reviews, and stock exchange transactions. The changes are part of a broader EU Economic Security Strategy, which emphasizes risk assessments around critical technologies, data access, and strategic inputs, with further measures expected on export controls, foreign subsidies, and outbound investment restrictions. Investors are advised to conduct early risk assessments and develop multijurisdictional filing strategies.

articles.title: European Commission to Unveil New Economic Security Doctrine Amid Rising Global Risks
articles.summary: The European Commission is set to unveil a new economic security doctrine on December 3, 2025, in response to escalating global risks, particularly from foreign economic coercion. The doctrine, which shifts focus from the 2023 strategy’s pillars of 'promotion, protection, and partnership' to 'protection and partnership,' will identify new risks in sensitive technological sectors such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies, and biotechnology. It will clarify how to respond to economic threats using existing EU trade tools—such as anti-subsidy measures, investment screening, and anti-dumping duties—without prescribing when to use them, as those rules are already codified in EU law. The document will outline specific countermeasures against foreign economic coercion, particularly targeting China and the United States, whose trade policies have pressured the EU, including the controversial trade deal signed in July 2025. The EU aims to transition from reactive to proactive risk management, with active involvement from European companies, which are seen as frontline actors in identifying real risks. The Commission also plans to strengthen its network across member states and foster partnerships with like-minded nations, including G7 countries, to assess risks in the evolving global trade landscape. High-level Brussels officials confirm that the instrument against foreign economic coercion, though discussed among member states, has not yet been activated.
